newsitem.title: UK: Britain ready for Zaire force once role clear.
newsitem.headline: Britain ready for Zaire force once role clear.

text.p: Britain remains prepared to take part in a multinational military force in Zaire if needed, junior defence minister Nicholas Soames told parliament on Wednesday.
But Soames said the situation was still confused and Britain and other western states needed more information before they could decide how to help refugees returning to Rwanda.
"Until we have more detailed information we will be in no position to take sensible decisions on how best to help," Soames told parliament in a hastily-arranged debate.
"In the meantime, we are continuing to plan a range of options with our potential partners in a multinational force."
Plans for a large-scale military intervention force have been scaled back since an estimated 500,000 refugees began a trek out of Zaire last Friday.
Rwandan Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana said on Tuesday that there were "hardly any" Rwandan refugees left in Zaire and there was no need for the multinational peace force.

British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, in Moscow for talks with Russian officials, told the BBC earlier: "I think a small number of troops any way will be necessary on a multinational basis to help the Rwandans with taking people across the border."
But Soames made it clear more information was needed before any force could be sent in.

Soames announced Britain was sending a photo-reconnaissance aircraft to the area to help get a better idea of what was happening on the ground and was also providing an extra 10 million pounds ($16.7 million) to help the refugees.
More than a million Hutus fled Rwanda in mid-1994 after it was overrun by Tutsi rebels, now in power, after the genocide of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus by Hutu extremists.

But last Friday, the same day the U.N. Security Council authorised a mission to get aid to the Rwandan refugees, 500,000 of them began a trek out of Zaire, taking a collective decision to leave their camps after the extremists who had terrorised them into staying were forced out by rebel Zairean attacks.
But there was uncertainty as to the fate of an estimated 500,000 refugees in the Bukavu area, south of Lake Kivu.

Local people have said some 7,000 people from Bukavu camp who tried to move northwards towards Goma last week to join the refugee flow home had been blocked by Hutus belonging to the Interahamwe militia halfway along Lake Kivu.

But tens of thousands more Hutu refugees were reported heading through eastern Zaire to Rwanda on Wednesday, the possible vanguard of a second mass exodus likely to finally kill off plans for the U.N. intervention force.
The U.N.'s World Food Programme (WFP) reported "strong indications" that at least 100,000 Hutu refugees still in eastern Zaire were on the move on Wednesday.
Soames told parliament that Britain was also in close touch with the humanitarian agencies.
"We are making absolutely certain that any contribution, whether military, political or in the form of aid, properly meets the need of the people in the region," Soames said.
Final decisions on a multinational deployment are expected after political talks this week in New York and a meeting of military planners in Stuttgart, Germany.
